claims.text: A machine-learning model trained on ab initio defect-containing configurations and experimental conductivity data can accurately predict electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The model can predict HfNbTaTiZr conductivity accurately in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Training configurations and measurements that include approximately 1 wt.% oxygen will make the model applicable to oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr.
The machine-learning approach will outperform analytical models that assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
The relevant samples contain realistic defect and impurity distributions.
Defect density and impurity scattering effects can be represented by combining ab initio defect calculations with experimental conductivity data.
The proposed applicability covers nominally pure and 1 wt.% oxygen HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Temperature-dependent defects and oxygen distributions modulate electron scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Machine-learning interatomic potentials can represent structural variation and disorder in multicomponent refractory alloys.
Machine-learning-guided interatomic potentials can explicitly capture electron scattering caused by defects and oxygen impurities.
Including temperature as a model input captures temperature-dependent electron scattering.
Representing disorder, impurity scattering, and structural variation yields more realistic conductivity predictions than perfect-crystal methods.
The model will closely match experimental conductivity measurements across both specified temperature regimes.
The model will reduce prediction error by more than approximately 20% relative to standard analytical methods.
Traditional analytical predictions fail to account for real defect distributions and oxygen impurity scattering.
Model reliability is limited to defect densities represented in training, oxygen contents up to approximately 1 wt.%, and the stated temperature intervals.
Extrapolation beyond the training composition or temperature range may reduce prediction reliability.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant error reduction greater than 20% relative to analytical models would falsify the hypothesis.
Predictions outside experimental uncertainty margins would falsify the hypothesis.
